## Laptops open

Working session. I am walking the room the whole time. And before we start:

**Something is going to break today.**

- It breaks in every section, every semester, for somebody
- It is never because that person is bad at this
- It is a version number disagreeing with another version number

- Fifteen minutes stuck, then raise a hand. Not thirty.

## What you walk out with

- Your own copy of the course workspace, on GitHub, named `mc451-workspace`
- That folder open in VS Code on your laptop
- A setup check that runs and comes back green
- One commit, pushed, visible on the web
- This is the **Project Setup** assignment, 25 points

## This folder is the whole semester

Every assignment from here lands in it. Your literature map, your codebook, your R scripts,
your final paper.

Set it up carefully now and you will not think about it again. Set it up carelessly and you
will be fighting it in Week 12, during the part that actually counts.

If your laptop dies in November, your work is on GitHub and you lose nothing.

## Idea one: a repository

A **repository**, or repo, is just a folder that Git is watching.

Nothing about it looks special on your computer. It is a folder with files in it. The
difference is that Git is keeping a record of every version of every file inside.

## Idea two: a commit

A **commit** is a snapshot. You take one whenever you have finished something.

It saves what every file looked like at that moment, stamped with the time and a short
message you write. You can return to any snapshot later.

**Push** sends your snapshots up to GitHub. **Pull** brings them back down.

## Idea three: render

**Rendering** is separate from all of that.

Quarto takes your `.qmd` file, which is plain text, runs the code inside it, and produces a
finished document with the results already dropped in place.

You write once, render, and you have something you could hand to a reader.

## Step 1: copy the course template

Go to the [v2v-workspace repository](https://github.com/AURA-Lab-SIUE/v2v-workspace).

- Click the green **Use this template**, then **Create a new repository**
- Name it `mc451-workspace`. Private is fine.
- Click **Create repository**

**You should see:** a page with your own username at the top and the same folders as the
template. You have not copied anything to your laptop yet.

## Step 2: clone it onto your laptop

- On your new repo, click the green **Code** button and copy the URL
- In VS Code press `Ctrl+Shift+P`, or `Cmd+Shift+P` on a Mac. A search bar drops down.
- Type **Git: Clone**, press Enter, paste the URL
- Pick a folder you will find again. `Documents/MC451/` is a fine answer.
- When VS Code asks, click **Open**

**You should see:** your folder names down the left side of VS Code.

## Step 3: let VS Code install the extensions

A box appears in the bottom right: **"This workspace has extension recommendations."**

Click **Install All**. That is Quarto, R, and GitLens, and it means everybody in this room
is working in the same environment.

If the box already vanished, press `Ctrl+Shift+X`, then search for and install **Quarto**
and **R** by REditorSupport.

## Step 4: open the file we wrote for you

In the workspace, open `00-check-your-setup.qmd`. It is also on the Hub and in your email.

You do not have to write it. You do not have to understand it. You click through it, one
grey box at a time, and it tells you what each box should print.

Start now. I am coming round.

## What "working" looks like

The file ends by running a checker we wrote for this course:

```r
library(v2v)
setup()
```

**You want:** green check marks all the way down **Required R packages**.

**Red next to Quarto or Git** is fine if you have not reached those steps yet.

**Red under Required** is the one that needs me. Wave.

*Talk it through with a neighbor while renders finish.*

## Step 5: your first commit

In VS Code's terminal:

```bash
git add .
git commit -m "Initial project setup with setup check"
```

`add .` gathers up everything you changed. `commit` writes the snapshot with your message.

**You should see:** a line reporting how many files changed. Write messages a stranger could
read: what changed and why, never "stuff".

## Step 6: push it

```bash
git push
git log --oneline
```

`push` uploads your snapshots to GitHub. `log --oneline` prints your history, one line each.

**You should see:** your commit message in the list, and the same files appear on your
GitHub page when you refresh it in the browser.

## The five errors you will actually hit

- **`quarto: command not found`.** Quarto is installed, but this terminal opened before it
  was. Close the terminal, open a new one.
- **`there is no package called 'v2v'`.** R is fine, the package is missing. Rerun step 3
  of the check file.
- **`fatal: not a git repository`.** You are in the wrong folder. `cd` into your workspace.
- **`nothing to commit, working tree clean`.** You did not save the file. Save, then `git add .`
- **Render fails on the YAML.** The `---` must be the very first line, nothing above it.

## When GitHub asks for a password

It will, and your password will not work. That is not a mistake on your part.

GitHub stopped accepting passwords for this in 2021 and wants a token instead. VS Code's
sign-in flow does the whole thing for you, once, and then never asks again.

Click through it when prompted. If it loops, wave at me rather than retrying.

For errors specific to our Twitch data, run `?v2v::common_errors`.
